sentences.text: Plesiosuchus was a geosaurine metriorhynchid crocodyliform that lived during the Late Jurassic in England and possibly Spain.
Researchers identified seven unique anatomical features in Plesiosuchus manselii that distinguish it from all other metriorhynchids.
Its teeth featured rectangular-shaped denticles and inconspicuous enamel ornamentation with low-relief ridges aligned from tip to base.
The largest known individual of Plesiosuchus is estimated to have been about 6.83 meters long, exceeding the estimated length of the pliosaur Liopleurodon ferox.
A referred specimen had a mandible measuring 132.2 cm, making it larger than the holotype which had a mandible of approximately 111 cm.

John Clavell Mansel-Pleydell discovered the type and referred specimens in the 1860s along the coast of Dorset. The type species, originally named Steneosaurus manselii, was first described by John Hulke in 1870.
Richard Owen established the genus Plesiosuchus in 1884 because he believed the species was more similar to modern crocodilians than to Steneosaurus.
A referred specimen showed an extreme reduction in tooth sockets, having only 13 alveoli compared to 19–25 in the related genus Machimosaurus.

Phylogenetic analysis places Plesiosuchus manselii at the base of the Geosaurini tribe in a polytomy with Torvoneustes and a clade containing Dakosaurus and Geosaurus. Plesiosuchus belongs to the parent group Plesiosuchina.
The closest known relative of the genus Plesiosuchus is the genus Suchodus.
The holotype was collected from the Lower Kimmeridge Clay Formation in Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset, dating to the late Kimmeridgian stage.
Fossil teeth attributed to Plesiosuchus were found in the Kimmeridgian-aged Tereñes Formation in Asturias, northern Spain.
